title: Lift up your heads (Luke 21:5–28)
hookLine: wars and signs; but when these things begin, look up

cards: Some people in the temple courts are admiring the building, and it deserved it: huge pale stones, gifts hung on the walls, a sanctuary still being finished and enlarged after decades of work.
Jesus looks at the same walls and says the days are coming when not one stone will be left upon another. His friends want details. When?
What sign? He doesn't give a date. He gives a long list of frightening things, and then an instruction about where to point your eyes.

teach.b: The list is hard to hear. Wars and commotions. Nation against nation.
Earthquakes, famines, plagues. Arrests and betrayals, even by family. Jerusalem surrounded by armies.
Signs in the sun, moon and stars, and the sea roaring.
Yet threaded through it are calm sentences: "Be not terrified." "There shall not an hair of your head perish. In your patience possess ye your souls."

Then the turn: "And then shall they see the Son of man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. And when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh."
When the news is terrible, the natural thing is to duck, to hunch, to stare at the ground. He tells them to stand up straight and look up.
Redemption, apolytrosis, was a word for buying back a captive or a slave: release, coming toward you. Christians read this chapter in more than one way.

teach.h: THE YEAR SEVENTY, AND THE DAY TO COME.
teach.b: Part of it, many say, came true within a generation: in the year seventy, Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple. Part of it, most Christians say, still waits for the day Christ returns.
Some read nearly all of it as fulfilled; others nearly all as future. Some have tried to pull dates out of it, but the chapter never gives one.

teach.h: LOOK UP, AND LIFT UP YOUR HEADS.
teach.b: It gives a posture: when the world shakes, lift your head.

how: Many churches read Jesus's words about the end in the season of Advent, when Christians prepare both for Christmas and for Christ's return, and they pray in the creeds that he will come again.

o: a ruin: stones thrown down from a wall
redemption: a captive bought back, set free
punishment: the debt a wrongdoer must pay

games.q: what's inside Luke 21:5–28 — tap the pairs.
p: look up, and lift up your heads

s: Jesus gives his friends a date for the end
he gives no date. he gives a posture: stand up, look up.
the temple in Jerusalem was destroyed by Roman armies
in the year 70, within about forty years of Jesus's words.
the chapter tells people to hunker down and hide their faces
it tells them to lift up their heads, for their redemption draws near.

games.q: wars, earthquakes, arrests, signs in the sky. everything is shaking. what does Jesus tell his friends to do?
o: work out the exact date from the signs.
look up, and lift up your heads.
games.why: "when these things begin to come to pass, then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh."

practice: Notice your posture right now; if you've been scrolling, your head is probably bent and your shoulders curled.
Breathe out, lift your chin a little, let your shoulders drop back, and look up at the ceiling or out at the sky for a few breaths.
Hold one thing that frightens you with your head up instead of down, and if you pray, bring it to God from there.

wordCard.voice: Apolytrosis, Greek for redemption, release by a ransom paid: not duck and hide, but stand straight and look up.

orig.note: Greek: redemption, release by a ransom paid. the word behind 'your redemption draweth nigh'.

carryVoice: Your line: your redemption draws near. Release, coming toward you, not away. Day five hundred seventy-five.
